tone_statements.citation: Amargira, Adelino. 2015. Number and case inflection in Tennet noun and adjective, a Surmic language of South Sudan. In Angelika Mietzner & Anne Storch (eds.), Nilo-Saharan: Models and Descriptions (Nilo-Saharan Linguistic Analyses and Documentation 28), 9-19. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. ISBN 978-3-89645-665-6.
tone_statements.quote: Tone carries an important function in the language, both lexically and grammatically. There are two level tones. In this paper, high tone is marked by acute accent and low tone unmarked but considered. The falling tone is marked by circumflex on the vowel. Rising tone is indicated by using two vowels with a low high pattern. [...] The suffix -i attaches to nominative singular nouns and the suffixes -a, -na attach to nominative plural nouns. A tone change from the tone of the accusative noun can mark both nominative singular and plural nouns.
tone_statements.locator: p. 10, end of section 2 'Tennet vowels'; second part p. 14, section 7 'Nominative case', followed by the tables 'Nominative singular noun tone changes' and 'Nominative plural noun tone changes'
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 level (H, L) + falling (HL) contour; rising treated as L+H on two vowels

sources.citation: Waag, Christine (with Adelino Amargira Alingor, Osfaldo Cirino Lomojo & Peter Bartholomeo Loromo). 2012. Tennet Grammar Book (adapted from the Laarim Grammar Book). First trial/draft edition, Feb 2012 (PDF Feb 2013). Juba: SIL South Sudan / Tennet Translation and Literacy Project. 114 pp. [= Glottolog ref 552814]
sources.note: Nothing. Literacy-oriented grammar (nouns, verbs, clauses, case/possessive suffixes); a full-text search for stress/accent/prominen = 0 hits in 114 pp. Only tone is treated: p. 20 'Tone is the difference in pitch, or how high or low the word sounds.. eez has Low [L] tone, but in (6), eez has High [H] tone.. do̱le̱c [H,HL] child has High tone on the first syllable.. and High-Low falling tone on the second'. Many entries flagged '(tone?)'.

sources.citation: de Jong, Nicky. 2004. Didinga orthography. OPSL 9: 145-162 (section 9 'Phonemes and graphemes in Didinga, Murle and Tennet', pp. 160-162)
sources.note: Nothing on Tennet stress; gives Tennet grapheme correspondences only ('Contrary to Didinga, the low vowel is also marked for ATR. The letter h only occurs word-medially'); Didinga described as 'a tonal language with two level tones'.

sources.citation: Randal, Allison. 2000. Does Tennet have postpositions? Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 8: 55-63 (TOC; Glottolog 57-66). Nairobi: SIL-Sudan. / Randal, Scott. 2000. Tennet's ergative origins. OPSL 8: 65-78 (TOC; Glottolog 67-80).
sources.note: Nothing about Tennet stress. The volume's only stress passages are in Gilley's Shilluk paper. The Tennet papers give only the orthographic tone convention (fn. 25: '[+ATR] vowels are underlined. High tone is marked with an acute accent, falling tone with a circumflex, and low tone is left unmarked') and tone-marked case (nominative marked by tone on some nouns).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tennet language' (wikitext; phonology section sourced to Randal 1995:5-11, 74; Randal 1998:220-221; Amargira 2011)
sources.note: No stress statement. Reports (second-hand from Randal) fortis/lenis consonants, 5+5 ATR vowels, contrastive length, and 'two level tones and a falling tone. A rising tone is treated as a low-high sequence, because it occurs only on long vowels.. Tone often marks grammatical relations and occasionally marks lexical distinctions' (citing Amargira 2011; Randal 1995:74).
